paragraphs.en: The pioneers of wireless saw it as a gift to all the people. Sir John Reith said that it would end "isolation of the spirit" and rejoiced: "It does not matter how many thousands may be listening, there is always enough for others…the genius and the fool, the wealthy and the poor listen simultaneously."
paragraphs.zh: 无线电广播的先驱们将它视为送给所有人的礼物。约翰·里思爵士说，它将终结‘精神上的孤立’，并欣喜地表示：‘无论有多少万人正在收听，总有足够的空间容纳其他人……天才与愚人、富人与穷人，都能同时收听。’

paragraphs.en: Between two great wars this technological innovation built a new kind of national consciousness. Opening this week, a book and exhibition curated by Beatty Rubens at the Bodleian in Oxford records how radio changed everyday life from 1922 to 1939. She draws on letters, diaries and fiction, and a 1939 field notebook of verbatim audience research by Winifred Gill.
paragraphs.zh: 在两次世界大战之间，这项技术创新塑造了一种新的国民意识。本周，一本书将问世，一场展览将在牛津大学博德利图书馆开幕；二者由比蒂·鲁本斯策划，记录了1922年至1939年间广播如何改变日常生活。她采用的材料包括书信、日记、小说，以及温妮弗雷德·吉尔于1939年开展听众研究时所作的一本逐字记录受访者话语的实地笔记。

paragraphs.en: There's fun in testimonies of people enjoying the sheer newness. A cartoon mocks a group failing to converse because they're all in headphones. People report that broadcast music made workmen whistle new tunes. A woman says there have been fewer street fights since the arrival of the wireless but also less stopping and "talking on the brush handle".
paragraphs.zh: 那些讲述人们享受这种全新事物的亲历描述充满趣味。一幅漫画讽刺了一群无法交谈的人，因为他们全都戴着耳机。有人说，广播音乐让工人们开始吹起了新的曲调。一位女士说，自从有了收音机，街头打架减少了，但人们停下来‘扶着扫帚把聊天’的情况也少了。

paragraphs.en: By and large the wireless was welcome. I loved the man from the Thirties research who found that wireless suddenly offered "a lot of variety…things I thought I'd never be interested in…ice hockey perhaps". True: for more than 80 pre-digital years, linear speech broadcasting brought the gift of serendipity, random enlivening of a car journey or dull manual task. In my own book about radio I recorded how, on one drive: "I caught up with the news, learnt some 17th-century history, and was startlingly educated by an unpretentious programme on the history of the stethoscope."
paragraphs.zh: 总体而言，广播受到了欢迎。我很喜欢20世纪30年代那项研究中一位男士的说法：他发现广播突然带来了‘各种各样的东西……一些我原以为自己永远不会感兴趣的事物……比如冰球’。确实如此：在数字时代到来之前的80多年里，按节目表依次播出的语音广播给人们带来了不期而遇的惊喜，随时可能为一段驾车旅程或一项枯燥的体力劳动增添趣味。我在自己写的一本关于广播的书中记录过，一次开车途中，‘我了解了最新新闻，学到了一些17世纪的历史，还从一个朴实无华、讲述听诊器历史的节目中收获了出人意料的知识。’

paragraphs.en: But radio's enriching serendipity is ebbing. With multiple networks and countless podcasts, a smartphone user selects what to hear and when. And while it is wonderful to take a walk with anything in your headphones, infinite choice encourages us to shrink into niche interests and sympathetic beliefs.
paragraphs.zh: 但广播带来的这种丰富生活的意外收获正在减少。面对众多广播网络和数不清的播客，智能手机用户可以自己选择听什么、何时听。尽管散步时戴上耳机就能收听任何内容确实很美妙，但无穷无尽的选择也促使我们退缩到狭窄的兴趣领域，以及与自身观点相合的信念之中。

paragraphs.en: A hundred years on from Marconi and Reith, is the art of mere listening endangered? Some will say the audiobook boom revives it, though I suppose you can then worry about the decline of reading. But inventions shape all of us and it is worth noticing when techno-social habits do change, and asking whether to control them a bit or shield the youngest. Whatever we do, innovation will happen. Today we fret about the isolating culture of smartphone-staring and selfie-vanity, but already in 1939 there was that lady regretting how, when all her street got wirelesses, it lost the neighbourly habit of "talking on the brush handle". It's enough to make a person put down the smartphone and go out front with a yard broom.
paragraphs.zh: 在马可尼和里思的时代过去一百年之后，单纯聆听这门艺术是否正面临危险？有人会说，有声读物的繁荣使它重新焕发生机，不过我想，这又会让人担心阅读的衰落。但是，发明创造塑造着我们所有人；当技术影响下的社会习惯发生变化时，我们值得留意，并思考是否应加以适当约束，或保护年纪最小的人。无论我们怎么做，创新都会发生。如今，我们为那种让人孤立的文化而忧虑：人们紧盯智能手机，沉迷于自拍带来的虚荣；但早在1939年，就已经有那位女士在惋惜，当她所在街道的家家户户都有了收音机之后，大家便失去了邻里间‘扶着扫帚把聊天’的习惯。这足以让人放下智能手机，拿起院子里的扫帚走到门前。
